implementation_notes: The stdlib answer is @functools.cached_property: the decorated method runs on the first attribute lookup and stores its result in the instance dictionary under the same name, so later reads never call it again, and deleting the attribute clears the cache. The decorator has not locked since Python 3.12 - the docs state that two threads can run the getter on first access and push the locking into the getter - so a shared stand-in either accepts an idempotent double build or guards itself. For module-level deferred attributes the equivalent is a module __getattr__ (PEP 562), and a plain @property plus a sentinel remains the hand-rolled form when the attribute must stay read-only or the class defines __slots__.
pitfalls: cached_property needs a mutable instance __dict__: it breaks on classes with __slots__ (without __dict__) and on metaclasses, and it interferes with key-sharing dictionaries so instances take more memory.
With the Python 3.12+ implementation there is no lock, so concurrent first access can construct the object twice; the getter must be idempotent or synchronize itself.
An exception leaves nothing cached, so every access retries the expensive construction - and if the result is mutable, every caller shares the same cached object.
